rationale: The best-known CRC stool signal is a group of oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, plus Gemella). Each one is sparse and low in abundance, and a random forest splits on only one genus at a time, so it can't easily pool these weak signals. This change adds a combined marker score (log of the markers' summed relative abundance) and a count of how many markers are present. These two features use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the four external CRC studies.

Many of the genus columns are rare and almost always zero, so they add noise. Because the random forest samples only about √p candidate features at each split, these columns crowd out the informative ones. This change keeps only genera present in at least 10% of the training fold's samples, computed inside `fit_predict` so no test information is used, and it always keeps the aggregated CRC marker features. The forest should then split on informative genera more often, and the filter works on taxonomy names, so it still carries over to the external studies.

Add one log-ratio feature: the CRC oral-pathogen markers measured against butyrate-producing genera that are depleted in CRC (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Butyricicoccus, Coprococcus, Lachnospira, Pseudobutyrivibrio). A ratio between two groups is a standard compositional-data feature. It doesn't depend on sequencing depth, and it combines a "gain" signal with a "loss" signal into one axis that a random forest can't build by itself, since it splits on one feature at a time. It uses taxonomy names only, so it should carry over to the external studies.

CRC stool is thought to have altered community structure (lower diversity, and a gut ecosystem disturbed by oral-pathogen colonisation). A random forest can't rebuild a whole-community summary from separate genus columns, so this change adds alpha-diversity features computed at the OTU level: Shannon and inverse Simpson on relative abundances, plus observed OTU richness after rarefying every sample to a fixed 5,000 reads with a fixed seed, so samples are compared at equal depth. These features are depth-normalised and don't use study-specific OTU identities, so they should carry over to the external studies.

I'm keeping the random forest and averaging its probabilities with an L2 logistic regression trained on CLR-transformed genus abundances. The forest splits on one genus at a time, so it can't easily capture the small additive shifts spread across many genera, such as oral pathogens rising while butyrate producers fall. A linear model on log-ratios captures exactly that. The logistic regression's regularization strength is tuned only by inner grouped cross-validation on the training fold, and both models use taxonomy names only, so the ensemble should still carry over to the external studies.

Right now every OTU without a genus assignment is merged into one `g__` column, no matter which family it belongs to. Many Baxter OTUs, especially in Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae and Porphyromonadaceae, have no assigned genus, so CRC signals going in opposite directions get mixed together. This change labels each unassigned OTU by its deepest named level (for example, `f__Lachnospiraceae;g__unclassified`), so those signals become separate features the forest can split on. The labels still use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the external studies.

This round adds family-level relative abundances next to the genus features, using the same training-fold prevalence filter. At genus level, many CRC-linked shifts are spread thinly over sparse, partly unassigned genera, for example the loss of several butyrate-producing Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae genera. Summing them by family should give the forest denser, less noisy columns to split on, and family names are the most consistent taxonomy level across studies, which should help on the four external studies.

The CRC signal in this cohort sits mostly in a few sparse oral-pathogen features. The default forest (√p features per split, leaves as small as one sample, about 230 training samples) may rarely sample those features and may overfit noise in the 100+ commensal genera. This change keeps the features the same and picks `max_features` and `min_samples_leaf` by inner grouped CV on the training fold only. A small grid is tested to see whether sampling more features per split and using smoother leaves ranks samples better.

I'm adding a second, wider panel of oral-pathogen genera alongside the existing core marker features: Solobacterium, Peptoniphilus, Anaerococcus and Campylobacter, which CRC meta-analyses (Wirbel 2019, Thomas 2019) report as enriched in CRC stool. Each is too sparse for the random forest to use on its own, so the panel gets its own pooled log-abundance and presence-count features. Keeping the original five-marker features unchanged means the wider panel can't weaken the core signal, and since it uses taxonomy names only it should still carry over to the external studies.

With only about 230 training samples and a CRC signal concentrated in a few sparse marker features, a 500-tree forest with fully grown trees produces noisy probabilities. Each tree samples only √p features per split, so it rarely picks up the markers. That noise blurs the ranking within each fold and the calibration across the pooled out-of-fold predictions. Raising the forest to 3000 trees, with the features and every other setting unchanged, should cut that noise and give a steadier risk score. It still uses taxonomy names only, so it should carry over to the external studies.

`marker_count` currently counts a marker as present whenever any read is seen. That depends on sequencing depth, which varies a lot within Baxter and even more across the external studies, so deeper samples score higher just by detecting more. This change replaces it with the expected number of markers that would be detected at a fixed depth of 5,000 reads. For each marker, the probability of detection is 1 − (1 − relative abundance)^5000, an approximation of the rarefaction expectation, and the feature sums these. It is smooth, deterministic and depth-independent, and adds no rarefaction noise.

The forest grows each tree independently and splits on one genus at a time, so it struggles to pick up the weak, interacting shifts spread across many commensal genera. This change averages the forest's probabilities with a shallow, strongly regularized CatBoost model trained on the same features. CatBoost builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the previous ones, and its ordered boosting is designed to resist overfitting on small samples like these ~230. Its errors should differ from the forest's, so the average should rank samples better. The features and filtering are unchanged and use taxonomy names only, so the model should still carry over to the four external studies.

I'm replacing the random forest with an extremely-randomized-trees ensemble (3000 trees, same seed and feature set) trained on log10-transformed genus abundances. Extra trees pick split thresholds at random. That makes their averaged probabilities smoother and less overfit than a random forest's on ~230 samples, so they should rank samples better. Because thresholds are drawn uniformly between a feature's min and max, the log transform is needed: without it, most thresholds would land in the long right tail of the skewed abundances. The features still use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the external studies.

Even after prevalence filtering, about 100 genus columns remain. Most of them carry no CRC signal, and because extra trees try only √p random features at each split, the few informative genera and the pooled marker features are rarely sampled. This change adds a label-aware filter inside `fit_predict`, computed on the training fold only: it keeps the 40 genera with the smallest Mann–Whitney p-values between cases and controls, plus the marker features, which are always kept. With fewer noise features, more splits should land on CRC-relevant taxa. Selection is by taxonomy name, so the model should still carry over to the external studies.

Family-level features failed in round 7 because, without selection, they simply added to the ~100 noisy columns. Now that round 14 added training-fold Mann–Whitney selection, this change pools genus and family abundances into one candidate set and keeps the top 40 by p-value. That way, family-level signals like the broad loss of Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae, or Porphyromonadaceae gain, that are spread thinly over sparse genera can come in only when they beat individual genera on the training fold. Family names are also the most consistent taxonomy level across studies, which should help on the four external studies.

Since round 14, the extra-trees model only sees the 40 genera that passed the Mann–Whitney filter plus the 2 marker features. The default √p setting therefore samples only about 6 of 42 mostly informative features per split, and the pooled marker features show up in only about a quarter of splits. This change raises `max_features` to one third of the features (about 14) so each split can usually pick a strong CRC feature. Extra trees draw random split thresholds, so the trees should stay diverse even with this greedier feature choice.

Picking the top 40 genera by Mann–Whitney p-value on about 230 samples is noisy, because genera ranked near the cutoff swap in and out depending on a few samples. To steady that choice, this change redoes the selection on 10 random 80% subsamples of the training subjects, grouped by subject. On each one it trains a 300-tree extra-trees model on the full training fold using that subsample's genera plus the marker features, then averages the probabilities. Strong genera will be picked every time, while borderline genera get included only some of the time, so no single noisy cutoff decides the ranking. The total is still 3000 trees, and everything uses taxonomy names only.

The individual CRC oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) are sparse. Right now each one can be dropped by the 10% prevalence filter or miss the top-40 Mann–Whitney cut in a given fold, which leaves only the pooled sum and count. This change always keeps each marker genus's own log abundance, so the trees can still use marker-specific signal: for example, a high Parvimonas level with no Fusobacterium means something different from the same total made up the other way round. The selection for every other genus is unchanged, and the features still use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the external studies.

This round adds co-abundance groups (CAGs) and keeps everything else unchanged. On the training fold only, the prevalent genera are clustered by Spearman co-abundance (average linkage, cut at 1−ρ = 0.7). Each group's summed log abundance becomes a candidate feature, and the 5 groups most different between cases and controls (Mann–Whitney) are added next to the 40 selected genera and the marker features. CRC shifts tend to happen across coordinated groups of genera, such as an oral-biofilm consortium or butyrate-producing commensals, rather than in single genera, and a summed group should be a denser and less noisy signal. Groups are defined by genus name, so they carry over to the external studies; I haven't run this yet, so there's no Dev score for it.

Clustering for co-abundance groups (CAGs) currently uses only genera present in at least 10% of samples. Many CRC oral-biofilm genera are sparse, including Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Gemella, Solobacterium and Dialister, so they never make it into a group. This change clusters genera present in at least 3% of the training fold, keeping the 10% filter for single-genus selection, so these taxa can form a co-occurring consortium from the data rather than a hand-picked list. Mann-Whitney selection of the top 5 groups on the training fold should then keep that consortium if it is informative and drop noisy rare groups.
